summary: Describes how DNS SRV records can be used to find email submission and access services. It updates RFC 1939 and RFC 3501. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6186 lets an email program use DNS to find the servers for sending and accessing mail. The program can use the domain in an email address to discover the server name, port and preferred mail-access service.

questions: how do mail clients discover servers with dns
how do mail clients find imap servers with dns
how does srv priority choose imap or pop3
what are the rfc 6186 srv service labels
subtitle: How an email program can discover submission and mailbox servers from the user's email domain.

tldr.problem: Mail programs often require users to enter a server name and port for each service. That setup differs across programs and can lead to errors.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6186 defines DNS SRV service labels for message submission, IMAP and POP3. A mail program looks up the labels using the domain from the user's email address to find server names and ports.
tldr.outcome: Users can configure an account with less manual server information, and SRV priority can express a domain's preference for IMAP or POP3. RFC 6186 updates RFC 1939 and RFC 3501 and is updated by RFC 8314 and RFC 8553.

today: RFC 6186 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011. It updates RFC 1939 and RFC 3501, and it has been updated by RFC 8314 and RFC 8553.

sections.title: Why Email Server Discovery Is Useful
sections.content:
Mail programs need servers for message submission and for accessing stored messages through IMAP or POP3. Users have typically entered a fully qualified server name and port for each service, and the setup differs between programs. Some programs instead probe the domain for available services.

RFC 6186 defines SRV service labels so a mail user agent can discover service details from the domain in the user's email address. This can reduce the information users must enter to an email address.
sections.plainLanguage: An email program needs to know which servers handle outgoing and stored mail. This RFC lets the program look up that information using the email address's domain.

sections.title: SRV Labels for Submission, IMAP and POP3
sections.content:
The submission label identifies a message submission agent and covers connections with or without TLS. The _imap label identifies IMAP where the server may require STARTTLS before authentication; _imaps identifies IMAP where TLS begins immediately on connection.

For POP3, _pop3 identifies a service that may require STLS before authentication, while _pop3s identifies a service that starts TLS immediately. The RFC gives example ports: 587 for submission, 143 and 993 for IMAP, and 110 and 995 for POP3.
sections.plainLanguage: Each mail service has its own DNS label. Separate labels distinguish services that may start TLS later from services that start TLS as soon as the connection opens.

sections.title: Using Priority to Express a Preference
sections.content:
A lower SRV priority number means a higher preference. A domain that offers both IMAP and POP3 should publish records for both and give the preferred service the lower priority. A mail program that supports both should look up both and use the service with the lowest priority.

If priorities are equal, the program may choose either service. If records for different protocols have different weights at the same priority, the client first chooses which protocol to use and then applies RFC 2782's weight algorithm to records for that protocol. A target of . marks a service as unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: The domain can use lower priority numbers to show which mail-access service it prefers. A target of a period tells the program that a service is unavailable.

sections.title: What a Mail Program Does with SRV Records
sections.content:
The mail program extracts the domain from the user's email address and queries SRV records for services it supports. A successful response supplies the server name and port. If no record exists, the program must ask the user for details or use another method. When several records exist, it follows their priority and weight.

For implicit TLS services such as _imaps and _pop3s, TLS begins on connection. For _imap, _pop3 and submission, the program uses STARTTLS or STLS as appropriate. When TLS is used, the program should send Server Name Indication and must verify the certificate using the SRV-based procedure in RFC 6125.

For authentication, the program first tries the full email address as the user identifier and should then try the local-part if authentication fails. After success, it should cache the server, port and user identity. A later retry should not switch between IMAP and POP3 without user interaction.
sections.plainLanguage: The program looks up the service, connects to the returned server and protects the connection before sending credentials when TLS is required. It remembers working settings, but does not silently switch between IMAP and POP3.

sections.title: What Service Providers Configure
sections.content:
Providers that offer this discovery method should configure IMAP, POP3 and submission servers to accept either the full email address or its local-part as a login identifier. These identifiers must not conflict with other permitted login names; local-parts must be unique across the server.

If a provider uses TLS, it must install a certificate that clients can verify using the SRV record as the starting point. If several domains share one IP address, the provider must support TLS Server Name Indication. The provider also installs SRV records for the services it offers.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers publish SRV records and configure their servers to accept the account names clients may use. They also need valid certificates and server-name indication when domains share an address.

sections.title: Protecting Credentials and Checking DNS Results
sections.content:
If a user requests a secure connection, the mail program must successfully negotiate TLS before sending any authentication command. An attacker who can alter DNS data or poison a recursive resolver could direct the program to an attacker-controlled server.

Without secure DNS, the program should check whether the SRV target belongs to the queried domain and ask the user before connecting to an unrelated target. When TLS is used, it must verify the server identity. Clients and servers must not request, offer or use SSL 2.0.
sections.plainLanguage: A false DNS answer could send a mail program to the wrong server. The program checks the target and verifies the server's certificate before sending the user's password.

data.title: SRV records
data.code:
_imap._tcp     SRV  0 0 0   .
_imaps._tcp    SRV  0 1 993 imap.example.com.
_pop3._tcp     SRV  0 0 0   .
_pop3s._tcp    SRV 10 1 995 pop3.example.com.
